In brief

Parody. "All those who are interested in the spread of human culture among the lower animals [...] And my guts red roaring / After Lowry's lights": newspaper writing is aped once more in response to a trivial human-canine interaction in the bar. The Citizen has been "talking about the Irish language and the corporation meeting and all to that and the shoneens that can't speak their own language." When Garryowen finds that his water tin is empty and starts nosing about inquiringly, the Citizen calls him over and "starts hauling and mauling and talking to him in Irish and the old towser growling, letting on to answer, like a duet in the opera. Such growling you never heard as they let off between them."

At more length

Anyone familiar with dog owners knows how most of them treat their loyal companions as if they can understand what they say, and how some dogs do their best to reciprocate with yips and growls and howls. The parody takes one of these everyday interactions as evidence of "the spread of human culture among the lower animals"—a "really marvellous exhibition of cynanthropy." Cynanthropy is a mythological term for shape-shifting between human and canine forms, as well as a psychiatric term for a form of insanity in which patients think themselves to be dogs. In this case the dog believes himself to be human and proves it by reciting eight lines of intricately structured Gaelic verse. The parody assumes that he is not only talking but speaking Irish, and that his utterances bear "a striking resemblance (the italics are ours) to the ranns of ancient Celtic bards."

Obviously the Gaelic League and the Irish Literary Revival remain targets here, but instead of imitating the tone of ancient manuscripts the prose now adopts the voice of a journalist hyping a public "exhibition of cynanthropy." The Citizen's amazing dog evidently can be viewed for a price, and readers "should make a point of not missing" it. Gifford correctly observes that Joyce is imitating "the style of a newspaper's plug for a theatrical program (not dissimilar to the 'paragraph' Bloom is trying to get to complement Keyes's ad)." Papers of Joyce's time frequently crossed the line between reporting and advertisement by inserting what Aeolus calls puffs—chatty little reports aimed at selling readers on a product or service. This particular puff pulls out all the stops, hinting at the "years of training by kindness and a carefully thoughtout dietary system" that have produced the Talking (and Poetry-Writing!) Dog, and coyly claiming that certain unnamed experts in ancient Irish poetry have verified the miracle.

One of these linguistic experts suggests that "the effect is greatly increased if Owen's verse be spoken somewhat slowly and indistinctly in a tone suggestive of suppressed rancour." Like the cat whose increasingly explicit vocalizations of her desire for milk are exquisitely rendered in Calypso, this dog says, with increasing impatience and a tinge of menace, but within the constraints of a "metrical system" that "recalls the intricate alliterative and isosyllabic rules of the Welsh englyn," that he urgently requires some water. "So he told Terry to bring some water for the dog and, gob, you could hear him lapping it up a mile off."

John Hunt 2026
